Cover why time series anomaly detection matters, the move from statistical methods to deep learning and transformers, why NAS fits, our guiding principles, and a bulleted contributions list.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Time series data is found in many sectors, from finance and healthcare to infrastructure and manufacturing, and this shows it has a pivotal role in modern analytics. This type of data is important for identifying patterns, dependencies, and anomalies that indicate significant shifts in system behaviors or the emergence of critical issues.

Traditionally, statistical methods have been the cornerstone of anomaly detection in time series data, and they are known for their robust mathematical frameworks. But Big Data, with its significant volume, velocity, and variety, has shown the limitations of these traditional methods, such as high false positive rates and missed detections.

In response, deep learning brought a paradigm shift, with better adaptability and performance in anomaly detection tasks. In particular, the transformer architecture with its self-attention mechanism has been a groundbreaking development, and it has made big strides in natural language processing and also in time series analysis.

Even with the advantages of transformer models, applying them to time series anomaly detection needs a more dynamic and adaptable framework to fine-tune their structures and parameters for optimal performance. Our model, TransNAS-TSAD, combines the architectural strengths of transformers (e.g., TranAD) with the optimization strategy of neural architecture search (NAS), so that a huge number of architectural configurations can be explored systematically. NAS uses the multi-objective optimization capabilities of the NSGA-II algorithm, which allows complex search spaces to be explored efficiently. This is a substantial evolution of the static architecture of TranAD, and it helps balance performance and computational efficiency.

  - transformer selective attention helps, if architecture tailored to research questions and dataset (cite)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Time series data is found in many sectors, from finance and healthcare to infrastructure and manufacturing, and this shows it has a pivotal role in modern analytics. This type of data is important for identifying patterns, dependencies, and anomalies that indicate significant shifts in system behaviors or the emergence of critical issues.

Traditionally, statistical methods have been the cornerstone of anomaly detection in time series data, and they are known for their robust mathematical frameworks. But Big Data, with its significant volume, velocity, and variety, has shown the limitations of these traditional methods, such as high false positive rates and missed detections.

In response, deep learning brought a paradigm shift, with better adaptability and performance in anomaly detection tasks. In particular, the transformer architecture with its self-attention mechanism has been a groundbreaking development, and it has made big strides in natural language processing and also in time series analysis.

Even with the advantages of transformer models, applying them to time series anomaly detection needs a more dynamic and adaptable framework to fine-tune their structures and parameters for optimal performance. Our model, TransNAS-TSAD, combines the architectural strengths of transformers (e.g., TranAD) with the optimization strategy of neural architecture search (NAS), so that a huge number of architectural configurations can be explored systematically. NAS uses the multi-objective optimization capabilities of the NSGA-II algorithm, which allows complex search spaces to be explored efficiently. This is a substantial evolution of the static architecture of TranAD, and it helps balance performance and computational efficiency.

Adapting anomaly detection models to time series data is complex in itself, especially for multivariate series, which have high-dimensional challenges and need sophisticated model architectures. The selective attention capabilities of the transformer model are a good solution, as long as the architectures are carefully tailored to the specific research questions and the characteristics of the dataset.

Bringing together NAS and multi-objective optimization algorithms like NSGA-II is a strategic evolution in automated model design. It gives a methodical way to discover optimal architectures that take into account multiple objectives that often conflict, and so it improves the adaptability and effectiveness of anomaly detection models.

Our research is based on three fundamental principles that address the challenges of time series anomaly detection. First, we stress that specialized models need to be developed for the specific temporal resolution and dimensional characteristics of time series data, so they are attuned to the details of temporal patterns. Second, we want to get the most out of transformer architectures and use their advanced capabilities for deep and nuanced interpretation of temporal data, which is critical for finding subtle anomalies. Last, strategic optimization with Neural Architecture Search (NAS), in particular using the NSGA-II algorithm, is the cornerstone of our methodology. It lets us refine our models systematically, so that they are highly effective and also optimized for the specific demands of the datasets they analyze. Together these principles guide us in creating models that are innovative and well adapted to the complex domain of time series anomaly detection. Our contributions are as follows:

- We introduce a new approach that applies NAS with NSGA-II optimization to fine-tune transformer architectures specifically for time series anomaly detection, which shows that NAS can adapt to specialized domains.

- Our experiments find key architectural configurations that raise detection performance, and this shows that architectural fine-tuning is important for model efficacy.

- We show substantial performance improvements on diverse datasets, showing that our optimized models are better than existing methods and that multi-objective optimization benefits anomaly detection.

- We get an optimal balance between computational efficiency and analytical accuracy, with models that are good at real-time anomaly detection and feasible to deploy in practice, so efficiency in model design is emphasized.

- Combining the structural strengths of transformers with the adaptive optimization of NAS gives uniquely effective models for time series anomaly detection, which is a significant advance that integrates architectural innovation with strategic optimization.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The ubiquity of time series data across various sectors, from finance [1] and healthcare [2] to infrastructure [3] and manufacturing [4], underscores its pivotal role in modern analytics. This type of data is instrumental in identifying patterns, dependencies, and anomalies that indicate significant shifts in system behavior or the emergence of critical issues [5,6].

Traditionally, statistical methods have been the cornerstone of anomaly detection in time series data and are renowned for their robust mathematical frameworks [7,8,9]. However, the advent of Big Data, characterized by significant volume, velocity, and variety, has revealed the limitations of these traditional methods, including high false positive rates and missed detections [10,11].

In response, deep learning has introduced a paradigm shift, offering enhanced adaptability and performance in anomaly detection tasks [12,13,14]. Notably, the transformer architecture, with its self-attention mechanism, has emerged as a groundbreaking development, making significant strides in natural language processing as well as in time series analysis [15,16,17].

Despite these advantages, applying transformer models to time series anomaly detection requires a more dynamic and adaptable framework for fine-tuning their structures and parameters for optimal performance [18]. Our model, TransNAS-TSAD, combines the architectural strengths of transformers (e.g., TranAD) with the optimization strategy of neural architecture search (NAS) to systematically explore a huge number of architectural configurations. NAS here leverages the multi-objective optimization capabilities of the NSGA-II algorithm [19,20], enabling efficient exploration of complex search spaces [21,22]. This is a substantial evolution of TranAD's static architecture, facilitating a balance between performance and computational efficiency.

Adapting anomaly detection models to time series data is inherently complex, especially for multivariate series that present high-dimensional challenges and require sophisticated model architectures [23,24]. The selective attention capabilities of the transformer model offer a compelling solution, provided that the architectures are carefully tailored to the specific research questions and dataset characteristics [25].

The convergence of NAS with multi-objective optimization algorithms such as NSGA-II marks a strategic evolution in automated model design. It provides a methodical pathway to discovering optimal architectures that account for multiple, often conflicting, objectives, thereby enhancing the adaptability and effectiveness of anomaly detection models [26,27].

Our research rests on three fundamental principles designed to tackle the inherent challenges of time series anomaly detection. First, we emphasize the need for specialized models tailored to the unique temporal resolution and dimensional characteristics of time series data, so that they are finely attuned to the intricacies of temporal patterns. Second, we aim to maximize the utility of transformer architectures, exploiting their advanced capabilities for deep and nuanced interpretation of temporal data, which is critical for identifying subtle anomalies. Lastly, strategic optimization through Neural Architecture Search (NAS), particularly using the NSGA-II algorithm, forms the cornerstone of our methodology, allowing us to systematically refine our models so that they are both highly effective and optimized for the specific demands of the datasets they analyze. Together, these principles guide our pursuit of models that are both innovative and highly adapted to the complex domain of time series anomaly detection. Our contributions are as follows:

- We introduce a novel approach that applies NAS with NSGA-II optimization to fine-tune transformer architectures specifically for time series anomaly detection, showcasing the adaptability of NAS in specialized domains.

- Our experiments identify key architectural configurations that elevate detection performance, highlighting the importance of architectural fine-tuning for model efficacy.

- We demonstrate substantial performance improvements across diverse datasets, showing the superiority of our optimized models over existing methods and the benefits of multi-objective optimization for anomaly detection.

- We strike an optimal balance between computational efficiency and analytical accuracy, presenting models that excel in real-time anomaly detection and are feasible for practical deployment.

- The synergy between the structural strengths of transformers and the adaptive optimization of NAS yields uniquely effective models for time series anomaly detection, a significant advancement that integrates architectural innovation with strategic optimization.
